title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Gillian Turner of Fox News
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Gillian Turner of Fox News Interview Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Jerusalem September 15, 2025 QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, thank you so much for taking time with us. SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you. QUESTION: You’re here in Israel as this major offensive in Gaza City is getting underway. To the outside world, it appears that this war is escalating rather than progressing towards a ceasefire and a hostage deal, as President Trump and yourself want. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. Well, how the war ends is the following: Every single hostage is released – all 48, including those that are deceased. Hamas no longer exists as an armed group threatening the strip. That’s how the war ends. So the question is how do you achieve it? And ideally, in a perfect world, you would achieve it through a diplomatic agreement. Hamas would agree to disarm and disband, and they would agree to immediately release every single hostage, including the bodies of those who have died. That’s the ideal outcome. That hasn’t come to fruition. So if it’s not going to end that way, then it’s going to have to end through a military operation. And I think the Israelis themselves would prefer it not be through a military operation. It’s – when we talk about defeating Hamas and going after Hamas, it’s Israelis that are going to have to go do that, not Americans. So we’re continuing to push, both – because I think that’s the goal President Trump has for this. He wants it to be over quickly, but he wants it to be over quickly with the hostages released, all of them, and with Hamas no longer being a threat. And so as much as anything else, this is about an opportunity to visit with our allies here in Israel to see what the plan is and what their ideas are for bringing that to fruition. QUESTION: When the President says that he is tired of these piecemeal hostage negotiations – he wants all of them to get released, the remainder of the hostages to get released all together – does that mean that you’re not longer going to negotiate along the lines of individual people? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, look, I think the President’s frustration about five hostages, eight hostages, ten hostages are widely shared, including by the hostage families. It’s just delaying and delaying and delaying. He’d prefer them – he thinks they all need to be – look, there shouldn’t be a single hostage. There shouldn’t be a single one. There never should have been a single one. So he wants them all released. That’s what he wants. Now, obviously, if they – it’s possible that some deal is arranged to where there’s the partial release for a 60-day period and then another group comes out – but that’s not what the President prefers. I think what he prefers is what we would all prefer, and that is every single hostage is released, every single one, including the bodies of those who are deceased because he’s – he, like a lot of people, have grown tired of seeing these drip, drip – slow releases, but still people being held. But there shouldn’t be a single hostage in a single tunnel anywhere in Gaza, but there still are. QUESTION: President Trump says he’s unhappy with the Israeli surprise strike on Doha. You yourself, sir, said that it could derail future negotiations, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said twice now that it was the right decision and he would actually make it again. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s a decision they’ve made, right, and he said that again today, that that’s a decision that came – it was an Israeli decision. And the consequences are owned by Israel as he, the prime minister himself, has said. What we’re focused on is what happens now because irrespective of what happened in Qatar last week, these facts remain: Hamas is still ensconced in parts of Gaza; 48 hostages are still being held, including 20 who are alive that need to be released immediately, all of them; and until – until those two things happen, it’s not going to be possible to have a Gaza that provides a higher quality of life for the people who live there and who are also being held in some ways as human shields by Hamas. So that – all those things remain. Irrespective of what happened in Qatar last week, in Doha, all of these things are still in place. We still have to deal with those. But – and we’re hopeful that Qatar will continue to play a positive and constructive role in helping bring this to an end. QUESTION: So Qatar is convening today, as you know, sir, this emergency session with its Gulf allies to come up with a response to those strikes. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look, I think there are — QUESTION: What would be the — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t think it’s a mystery that they’re not happy about what happened. They’ve shared that with us. We met with their prime minister – the Vice President and I did last Friday. We then had dinner that evening. the prime minister did, with the President. And we’re visiting again with them very shortly here in the next day as well. So we understand they’re not happy about what happened. I think our message is irrespective of that, and that’s one thing, we need to separate that from the fact that no matter what, we still have Hamas, we still have hostages, and we still have a war. And all those things still have to be dealt with, and we are hopeful that Qatar and all of our Gulf partners will continue to add something constructive to bringing this alternate –it’s in their interest that this war end as well. QUESTION: Are you concerned, Mr. Secretary, that by traveling to Doha while they are holding these meetings, the prime minister here is going to feel – not snubbed because you just met with him, but feel sort of put upon? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, look, our relationship with Israel is not going to be affected by any of this. We’re going to continue to be strong allies and partners. But the President has – the President said he wasn’t happy the way things went down. That doesn’t mean we’re going to stop being their partner and their ally. As far as meeting – well, we met with the Qataris already. What – we have – we have military bases there. We’ve cooperated on a host of issues with Qatar, and we’ll continue to do so as well. So – but our message both here in Jerusalem and also in Doha will be what it’s been consistently, and that is despite – we’re not diminishing it. We’re not asking them to ignore it. We understand they’re upset about it. We understand the Israeli position on it. Irrespective of that, we still have hostages that we want released. We still have a Hamas that needs to be defeated or eradicated or removed so that we can get to the peace that everybody says they want. And so we’re trying to get everybody to stay focused on what happens moving forward, not just only focused on what’s already happened with – what happened last week in Doha. We want everybody focused on what comes next because we still have these problems we have to solve. QUESTION: One thing that comes next, at least for the Israelis, sir, is they are talking about their new plans to move ahead with annexation of the West Bank. Is that something the Trump Administration is supportive of? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we’re not commenting on that now other than to say that we warned all these European capitals and other countries that if they went ahead with this Palestinian state recognition, which really is symbolic more than anything else – they’re responding to their own domestic politics – we warned that there would be a response to that, that, number one, it would make it harder to reach a peace deal in this Gaza war because it would embolden Hamas, and it has. And the other thing we warned is it would force Israel to now do things in reaction to that. And I think part of this conversation about annexation is in response to what’s been coming out of Europe, Canada, and other countries with a Palestinian statehood move which is largely symbolic, but yet has these real-world implications in terms of making it harder to achieve peace. We thought it was counterproductive. We shared that with them at the time. They did it anyways. And we’re seeing – I think this talk of annexation is part of that. QUESTION: Switching gears to Russia, there have been two Russian drone incursions into Poland and then Romania this week. It appears President Putin is emboldened after his meeting with President Trump in Alaska. SECRETARY RUBIO: Look, I wouldn’t say he’s emboldened after the meeting. I would say that this is an example of why this war the President thinks needs to end. Wars generally will escalate. They’ll actually get worse, not better if they continue on the track their on, especially a protracted war like this one which – given that both sides are deeply dug in. I understand that these drone operations are far from the front lines. They have no impact on the front lines. They’re designed largely to weaken one another. And the Ukrainians are conducting strikes in Russia as well. And it’s one of the reasons why the President has said he wants this war to end. This war should end. It’s why he’s expended a tremendous amount of political capital, energy, and time in trying to bring it about to an end. No one in the world has done more to end – to try to end the Ukraine-Russia war than President Trump has. But ultimately, it takes the two sides who are fighting to agree to it. And as you’ve said and as you’ve pointed out, we haven’t been able to get those kinds of results from the Russian side. But again, that’s not Trump’s war. Trump inherited this war. And now President Trump is doing everything he can to try to bring it to an end. QUESTION: So how much longer will the President give Putin before he moves forward with the sanctions that have been threatened? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we fully understand the sanctions that we have available to us, and at some point the President may decide to do that. That’ll be his decision to make. He’s not going to go around and artificially announce a time frame. But he’s also pointed out that it’s important for Europe to do so as well. There are still countries in Europe that are buying Russian products, including Russian oil. And what the President has challenged our European partners is to impose the sanctions themselves that they’re asking us to impose. So if they feel deeply committed to this, they should take – we want to encourage them to actually do the things they’re asking us to do. QUESTION: Closer to home, sir, Brazil. Former President Bolsonaro has been sentenced now, this obviously over the objections of the President. You yourself, sir, called the trial a witch hunt. What’s the U.S. response? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, the response there is that the rule of law is breaking down. You have these activist judges – one in particular – that not only has gone after Bolsonaro, by the way, he has tried to – he’s tried to carry out extraterritorial claims against even American citizens or against someone posting online from within the United States, and has actually threatened to go even further in that regard. So there’s going to be a U.S. response to that, and that’s what – we’ll have some announcements in the next week or so about what additional steps we intend to take. But it – it’s not – the trial is but a – one more chapter of a growing sort of judicial oppression campaign that has tried to reach American companies, and even people operating out of the United States. QUESTION: On Venezuela, sir, you’ve – the State Department put up this bounty on Nicolás Maduro. The administration took out that boat of narcotraffickers, I believe last week. Are you any closer to capturing him? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, there’s no bounty on Nicolás Maduro. What it is, is a reward for an indicted person – here’s what people forget, okay? Nicolás Maduro was indicted by the Southern District of New York. A grand jury returned an indictment. They read the evidence – they saw the evidence. They returned an indictment, not just against him personally but against a network of people in that country who used the apparatus of what they claim to be a government to conduct drug trafficking operations against the United States. So there’s a reward for his capture, and it’s out there and it’s available, and it was increased. That’s what that’s a consequence of. In addition to that — QUESTION: Are you not concerned, sir, that it gives the impression of advocating for some kind of regime change or (inaudible) that — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, he’s not a – but the thing is they’re not – he’s – we don’t – not only do we not recognize him, 50-something countries around the world do not recognize Nicolás Maduro as the rightful president. He’s not the president of Venezuela. That’s a title he’s given himself. And that’s not just us saying it. That was – by the way, that was the policy of the Biden administration, and that was the policy of the first Trump Administration, and that’s the policy of 50-something countries, including multiple countries in the region, do not recognize him as the president of that country. What he is, is someone who’s empowered himself of some of the instruments of government and are using that to operate a drug cartel from Venezuelan territory, much of that drugs aimed at reaching the United States. So we’re not going to have a cartel, operating or masquerading as a government, operating in our own hemisphere. He’s indicted. He’s a fugitive of American justice. There’s a reward out for his capture. And by the way, related to that, the President of the United States made clear that he’s not going to allow cartels, that cartel or any other cartel, to operate with impunity in our hemisphere and send drugs towards the United States. And he’s going to use the U.S. military and all the elements of American power to target cartels who are targeting America. QUESTION: Are you concerned at all about the optic that the Trump Administration is meddling in the internal affairs of a sovereign country, especially in the Western Hemisphere, where there’s a history of it? SECRETARY RUBIO: But when you traffic drugs into the United States, you’re meddling into the internal affairs of America. When you are pushing drugs towards the United States of America, you are a direct threat to the national security and the national interest of the United States, and that’s what we’re addressing here. QUESTION: What about reporting, sir, that that boat with the drug traffickers had turned around at the point which it was struck? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know where those reports are coming from, and I don’t even know if that’s accurate. But I can tell you that irrespective – there’s a network. And the way this network runs is speedboats with multiple 350-horsepower engines, four of them. They carry drugs to somewhere in the Caribbean. From there, they jump to Puerto Rico. And from Puerto Rico, obviously now they’re in the United States; they’ve crossed the border. So this is the network, the route that they run. We have 100 percent fidelity and certainty that that boat was involved in that trafficking of those drugs that ultimately were destined to reach the United States of America. And the President’s made clear: Interdiction alone is not going to stop these drug traffickers. They don’t mind losing 2 percent or 3 percent of their shipments. They’ve already sort of baked that into their economic plan. What needs to start happening is some of these boats need to get blown up. Some of these boats need to be not just intercepted but stopped, no matter what direction they plan to head. We can’t live in a world where all of a sudden they do a U-turn and so we can’t touch them anymore. And I’ll tell you something: Since we did that, the number of boats heading towards the United States suddenly dropped dramatically. Now, maybe they won’t be sustained or continued, but we’re not – and the President’s made clear – we are not going to continue to allow these cartels to flood the United States with drugs, be it through the water or through land. QUESTION: A question on Charlie Kirk, sir. The – his assassination is highlighting the threat of political violence in this country, which people seem to be in agreement is on the rise. Do you share that assessment, and do you believe that it’s only a problem emanating from the left? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think here’s the bottom line, and that is if you look at President Trump, those efforts to assassinate him not once but twice, yes; there was an attack against elected officials in Minnesota as well earlier this year, and we saw that. We saw the assassination of Charlie Kirk in front of the whole world. And I would say what’s most stunning about Charlie and what happened to him – look, for a lot of people in the White House, myself included, this wasn’t just a political assassination. It was the assassination of someone we knew personally, someone we’ve gotten to know, someone many of us have worked with in the past who we knew as a person, not just as a figure. It doesn’t make it any less tragic, obviously, but it makes it even sadder. But the irony with Charlie is that what he was doing was engaging those who disagreed with him in debate, in the kind of conversation that we need to be having in American politics. Some of these are very contentious issues. But the alternative to violence is the ability to debate through them. And that’s what he did, not just on college campuses but in podcasts, in interviews. He would go on shows. He would go on the shows of people who he disagreed with. And for him to be assassinated for doing that I think was not just an attack against Charlie Kirk but was an attack against this willingness to engage in political debate in this country. So I do think it has the potential to have a chilling effect, and we can’t let it have that impact because it’s a – that is a direct threat to our – not just our democracy but our freedom of speech and our ability to communicate in this country. QUESTION: Your deputy has been calling out on social media foreigners who he says are celebrating, glorifying, Charlie’s murder. Do you have any plans to restrict visa access — SECRETARY RUBIO: Sure. QUESTION: — or even revoke visas? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, and here’s why. A visa, okay, it’s different from being a U.S. citizen. A visa means you’re a visitor. You’re a visitor to the United States. We are not in the business of inviting people to visit our country who are going to be involved in negative and destructive behavior, okay? So why should – if I invite someone – if we invite someone to visit the United States of America as a student, as a tourist, as whatever, then they have a different – the standard they should be held to is very high. We shouldn’t be bringing people into this country – we should not be giving visas to people – who are going to come to the United States and do things like celebrate the murder, the execution, the assassination, of a political figure. We should not – and if they’re already here, we should be revoking their visa. Why would we want to bring people into our country that are going to engage in negative and destructive behavior? It makes no sense. QUESTION: I wanted to be mindful of your time. Is there anything else that we didn’t touch on that you would like to talk about? Or — SECRETARY RUBIO: No, we touched a lot. title: Secretary Rubio’s Meeting with Prime Minister Kristersson
text: hide Secretary Rubio’s Meeting with Prime Minister Kristersson Readout Office of the Spokesman May 22, 2026 The below is attributable to Spokesperson Tommy Pigott: Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson in Helsingborg, Sweden following the NATO Foreign Ministers Meeting. The two leaders agreed on the importance of increasing bilateral defense cooperation, including strengthening the transatlantic defense-industrial base. After the meeting, Secretary Rubio and Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard signed the U.S.-Sweden Technology Prosperity Deal, which will enhance scientific and technical cooperation across AI, biomedical, quantum, advanced manufacturing, space, and other critical fields. title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Joint Base Andrews, Maryland July 19, 2026 QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, can I ask you a question? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: You were just at the final of the Spanish-Argentina. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: I wanted to ask your thoughts. And are you converted to football? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m very – am I what? QUESTION: Have you converted to football? SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, I’ve always been a fan of it. I’m an admirer. It’s a global sport. Look, first of all, I’m very – and congratulations, obviously, to Spain. We had time today to spend with both the president and His Majesty the King and Queen. I have a lot of friends from Argentina, so obviously sad for them. But I am very proud of America. I think America did a phenomenal job hosting the games. So did Canada and Mexico. And I hope a lot of people who got to come here and visit got to see aspects of our country that I think sometimes we take for granted – things about our nation that are so special that sometimes I think those of us who have lived here our whole lives maybe forget or take for granted. So I was on the phone on the way up here wondering when the – when’s the next one we can bid on is, because it was such a spectacular event for the country. And so I’m very happy about it. QUESTION: Secretary, last week the President talked about China’s meddling in the 2020 U.S. election. Is the visit by President Xi Jinping that he had mentioned around September 24th, is that still on track? And is the strategic stability relationship between the U.S. and China, the trade (inaudible), are those things still on track despite this evidence that the President has mentioned? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I mean, we anticipate that the trip is happening in September. They’ve continued to send over their teams to prepare for it, and I’ve heard nothing otherwise. I have no reason to believe that they won’t be coming. It’s important. There will always be – when you have two big, powerful countries like the United States and China, there are always going to be irritants, there are always going to be things we don’t agree on, but I think it’s incumbent on powerful and important countries like ours to continue to talk and have a relationship. We owe it to each other and for our people and to the world. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, we’re on the ninth – the ninth day straight of strikes now with Iran. Iran is launching these strikes. Are we back at square one, and what is the objective of these latest strikes? SECRETARY RUBIO: I think CENTCOM has laid it out exactly what the objectives are. The only reason why the U.S. is conducting strikes is against assets of Iran that are being used to attack global commercial shipping. The Straits of Hormuz are an international waterway, and they continue to launch against ships in that international waterway. Other countries should join us in this effort, but the United States is involved not just in protecting those ships but in targeting the places that they use to launch these missiles and drones. So that’s what you’re seeing. That’s what the objective of this mission is. That’s what it continues to be. And we continue on a daily basis very successfully to degrade Iran’s ability to target (inaudible) ships. You hear about the ships that have been struck. You don’t hear about the ones that have been defended and the ones they haven’t been able to launch against. QUESTION: Do you — SECRETARY RUBIO: But as long as Iran insists on controlling an international waterway, we’re going to have to respond to that. QUESTION: Do you see a diplomatic off-ramp still? Do you believe that we — SECRETARY RUBIO: I think we’re always open to diplomacy. It has to be real. It has to be a deal that they’re willing to live by. Look, Iran a week ago was supposed to put out a statement saying that the Straits of Hormuz would be opened and that they would no longer attack shipping. And instead of doing that, they attacked three ships. I think that was last Friday or Saturday. So I mean, their behavior has to change in order for ours to change. QUESTION: Is the MOU dead? QUESTION: (Inaudible) the MOU? SECRETARY RUBIO: What? QUESTION: Is the MOU dead, or are we just back in full-scale war? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, they’re not complying with it. I mean, the straits are supposed to be open – free of tolls, free of attacks, free of all the things they’re doing against these ships. So they’re – you can’t have an MOU that’s alive if they’re violating the terms of it. What I will say is that the United States always remains open to a diplomatic solution, and we’ve tried multiple times with Iran, and we’ll continue to try. If that door opens, we’ll be happy to see it open. But right – and they continue to send signals that they want to talk, that they want to negotiate, but their behavior is what we’re responding to. And their behavior is they’re launching missiles and drones at ships, including tonight. QUESTION: What recent signals have you heard from the Iranians that they want to negotiate? SECRETARY RUBIO: Directly and through multiple channels with other countries as well. They continue to send signals that way. But like, I also think it’s pretty growingly apparent, it’s growing apparent, that even within their own system there’s a growing split – I think maybe some of (inaudible) have documented this – between those that understand that their economy is in shambles and they need to do something or they’re going to be in a lot of trouble very soon economically and domestically, and others who are very militant in their view of life and in their view of the world and continue to launch missiles. So they’ll have to work out that split internally. We’re going to continue to respond. If the door opens to diplomacy, if the guys that want to do something productive for Iran win and take control of that system or take control of the negotiations, that’ll be a very positive development. That’s not where we are tonight, unfortunately. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, what is your main goal? You’re headed to Southeast Asia. What do you want — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, this summit, ASEAN, is our primary way of engaging the region. We’re committed to it. I was there last year. I also went with the President when he went to the Leaders’ Summit, and we’re returning again this year. And it gives us an opportunity not just to participate in this gathering but also to do a lot of bilateral meetings. We’ll also have meetings with the Quad of India, Australia, Japan, and ourselves. We’ll also have a trilateral meeting with South Korea and Japan, which is another forum we’ve pursued. I think we’ll have an opportunity potentially to meet with the foreign minister of Vietnam and a couple other countries. Obviously, I’ll also have a chance to visit with the president there in the Philippines. This is a country I have not yet visited as Secretary of State. So it’s a long way to go. We appreciate you guys joining us on the trip. But it’s an important forum for us. QUESTION: Will you meet with the Chinese — QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, can you give us an update on Venezuela, and in terms of the rebuilding and reconstruction effort in Venezuela following the earthquake? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: What’s the U.S.’s commitment to Venezuela at this point given — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, it’s already upwards of $180 million and we’re looking – we’ll do more. The Venezuelans will do more. I think we’re trying to help them get access to global funding and credit as well for their rebuilding. They’re still working through an estimate on the total cost, and it’ll be substantial – both removal of the debris and building new things. By the same token, very good news last week. I thought it was a little bit under-reported, to be frank. And that is that a group representing the 2015 national assembly, the last democratically elected national assembly, the group that we recognized as the legitimate government of Venezuela, had a meeting with the interim government, and they have agreed to set up a format and a forum not just for reconciliation talks but to begin the transition process, which is what the people of Venezuela need. I think their first official talks will begin the first week of August. I thought that was a very powerful offer. And obviously, we’ll see where it goes, but we think that that agreement was broadly met in Venezuela as very good news, and obviously something we’re going to be very engaged in. QUESTION: Do you plan to meet with the Chinese foreign minister or Lavrov while you’re out there for the ASEAN Summit? SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m not sure we’ve finalized that, but we’d be open to meeting with him, sure. QUESTION: And would you bring up anything about the Chinese election meddling claim that Trump made? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I would never tell you guys in a press conference what we would raise in meetings like that. Those are delicate matters. QUESTION: Do you think it’s important to? SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, we’ll see what the – we’ll see how the meeting goes. We’ll talk about things that are important, certainly. QUESTION: And — SECRETARY RUBIO: We gotta – we want to go, guys. But what else? QUESTION: And what was your reaction to the President saying he wanted to charge a 20 percent toll on cargo going through the — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, but I think what the President was implying, what the President was saying basically, is that the United States, okay, every night is taking on the burden of protecting global shipping. Virtually none of those vessels are flagged U.S. Almost none of those vessels are delivering cargo or fuel to the United States. So we are basically providing the service of protecting these ships on behalf of the world, and we’re the only ones doing anything about it. So what the President is basically raising the point is, at some point, the countries and the nations benefitting from shipping through the straits should be able to step forward and provide at least financial assistance to the cost of providing this very valuable service. That’s what the President was alluding to. Now, he pointed out after the fact as well that some of the countries who are shipping products through the straits are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in the United States, and he’ll credit that, for example, as far as investments. But I do think the world is coming to a point now where it’s clear that Iran – at least some people in Iran – want to control the strait and hold that as leverage against the world. And the world has to decide whether or not it’s going to allow an international waterway to be under the control of a country like this. It’s completely illegal, unlawful, and unacceptable. The United States will do and continue to do what it needs to do to protect global shipping, but other countries need to begin to step up and provide – whether it’s hardware or finances to help carry that burden. It is not the United States’ job to protect shipping for the entire planet forever. QUESTION: What is the word on these investments that Trump said Gulf countries would be doing for – in exchange for protection in the strait? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, some of those investments have already been committed to, and there are others that we believe they’ll commit to in the future. But obviously, a lot of that is dependent on the health and the vibrancy of their own economies. They have to be able to generate revenue in order to make these investments, and they won’t be able to do that if the oil and natural gas isn’t getting to the marketplace. QUESTION: You saw the leaders of Mexico and Canada today at the World Cup. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, we had a good time with them. QUESTION: Were there discussions at all about policy, or was it entirely — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I can’t speak to everything. I know the President had some conversations that I wasn’t privy to with them. But for the most part, it sounded to me like three countries that did a good job working together hosting the World Cup with Canada and Mexico. The cooperation was extraordinary. I think they were just having a good time and there’s good chemistry, especially with President Sheinbaum. Obviously, we have some issues with Mexico that are very difficult and important for us, but I don’t think the World Cup game was probably the best place to discuss it. But we were glad she came, and we’re glad the prime minister came as well. QUESTION: Can you tell us about your meeting with the Lebanese president today? SECRETARY RUBIO: Very positive this morning. I think, as I said, the future of Lebanon, the best thing that could happen to Lebanon, is to have a government, a legitimate government, his government, that controls the country. The biggest problem Lebanon has is that you have a political movement that also has an armed militia that is not just well armed and trained and equipped and financed by Iran, but they use that to conduct terrorism, particularly against northern Israel. And as long as that problem exists, Lebanon will never fully be at peace. And so how do you defeat Hizballah? How do you replace Hizballah? You defeat and replace them with a government that is strong enough to be the sole force of arms in the country, basically with the security of Lebanon in the hands of the Lebanese Armed Forces, and a government that’s able to provide prosperity for its citizens. So we talked about the opportunities to do that. This is not just about military stuff. This is about how can we attract more U.S. and international investment into Lebanon. This is about things like how can we restart direct flights between the United States and Lebanon that are – right now, you can’t do that. So we’re going to start a process with them and see if that’s possible and when that can be done. So we had a good meeting, and I think he’ll leave on Tuesday. He’ll have a very positive meeting with President Trump. And I think President Aoun will be able to return to Lebanon and say to the people of Lebanon that he is the one that’s getting positive results for the people – all Lebanese, including Christians, Sunni, and Shia, and Bedouin and Druze – all the people of a very diverse country – not Hizballah, not Iran. He is the legitimate government, he is who we’re going to work with, and that government is the government that should be in charge of that country. All right, last one. QUESTION: If the factions in Iran that are working for diplomacy, if they don’t win out, what next? What happens? And do you have a message for — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t think it’ll be good for Iran. I mean, Iran’s economy is in shambles, right? Three hundred percent inflation, particularly on life-sustaining goods. They have dwindling revenues to meet even their own payroll. They have food shortages. They have a drought, which we didn’t cause. But they have a gasoline shortage and a fuel shortage. All these problems existed before all this began. They’ve just gotten worse. They will continue to get worse. And one of the reasons why Iran is in shambles – this is a rich country. Iran is a rich country. One of the reasons why Iran is in shambles is because every penny that this regime there gets, be it in sanctions relief or through the oil they’re able to get out, they invest it in Hizballah, they invest it in Hamas. They spent billions of dollars supporting militias in Iraq, Hizballah, and Hamas. They’re not – they should be spending billions of dollars supporting the people of Iran. They should be spending on things like building their country. But instead they use it to sponsor terrorism. So I think there’s a growing awareness of that inside of Iran, and I think there’s even a growing awareness of that amongst some of the people in their government. In fact, we have heard that from some of the people in their government. But obviously, there’s a tension there and we’ll see how that plays out. I can’t tell you how it’s going to play out. It’s up to them. QUESTION: Any message on the fallen troops, sir? The fallen troops? SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, yeah. Look, obviously, I think sometimes when you look at this stuff we forget, we take for granted, that our military is so effective, but the mission they carry out is very, very dangerous. And so we lost people in Jordan after there was a strike. A missile got through. We shot down almost all the missiles. One leaked through, hit the wrong place, and tragically, and it’s heartbreaking. And our hearts go out to the families of the heroes that paid the ultimate price. We also lost a service member in Iraq unrelated to combat. They were decommissioning ammunition and an accident happened in that process and they were harmed. But look, our military all over the world, especially in that part of the world but all over the world every single day, do very dangerous things. We’ve had people who have lost their lives in training. Nothing the military does is safe. It’s all inherently dangerous. And we’re just grateful to have such heroic Americans in uniform in service of our country. And obviously, it goes without saying that we’re praying for their families and praying for their souls. We are grateful that we have people like that serving us, both those who we have lost and those who at this very moment are on the watch defending our interests around the world. title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State U.S. Embassy Quito Quito, Ecuador September 9, 2026 SECRETARY RUBIO: All right, let’s go. Hold on. QUESTION: Secretary Rubio — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: Can I – are you worried at all that U.S. partnership with Ecuador and some of the accusations of human rights abuses or disappearances will undermine and – the U.S. partnership with Delcy Rodríguez in Venezuela, Bukele and some of his accused abuses – will undermine the goodwill that you guys are — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, but all these governments are – for example, Ecuador is going to get attacked by left-wing groups that have ties to terrorists. These groups – you know the brutal – the real human rights violations happening in this part of the world is on behalf of narcoterrorists and this web of narcoterrorists who, like – they cut people’s heads off; they decapitate people. They go through and they extort people, like small vendors, in these towns, in these cities, in these countries. These vendors – that used to happen – in El Salvador you couldn’t even run a small coffee shop. They’d come in an extort you for money or they’d kill your children. These are the real human rights violator; these are the real terrorists. And these are the people that are being dealt with. And you have to deal with these people in a very strong way, and that’s who we’re aligning with. We are aligning with governments and leaders that are willing to be serious about taking these groups on, as opposed to leaders who in the past, like we had with Petro in Colombia, are actually on the take or aligned with these terrorist organizations and these narco groups and so forth. So you have to make a choice here. We’re going to choose on the side of leaders that are going to be serious about taking these groups on and eliminating them once and for all. Otherwise, those groups – those terrorist groups – will eat these countries up. They will become stronger than the governments in these countries. They will run over these countries. So I’m glad we have leaders in the region that are willing to be strong and take these groups on. QUESTION: What about — QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, there’s a sense out there – an impression, I guess – that the strategy, the actual strategy towards combating these groups, and especially on the water, has changed a bit from where, when it began, it was just you blew the ships out of the water. And now it seems that you intercept them first, stop and get the people off, and then — SECRETARY RUBIO: It depends. QUESTION: Then sink them. So (inaudible). SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, it depends. So it depends on the country. So for example, with – no, because in many of these, these are bilateral operations. They’re – they’re occurring, for example, in territorial waters. So when you cooperate with Ecuador – they’ve been very cooperative – we’re jointly operating with them. So it depends on the vessel; it depends on the threat it poses; it depends on where it’s located. But these are part of the bilateral agreements we have with these countries, which is an – I think an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters. And then obviously we have to operate according to their laws in their territorial waters or their systems and protocols that they set in place. The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended. QUESTION: Right. But does that mean that these countries – it’s more palatable or legal for these countries to do it in this way, stopping the ship, getting the people off, and returning them to the — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, again, it depends – and we still blow-up ships if need be. QUESTION: No, I know, but they’re empty now. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, again, it depends. Every target is selected. Obviously it goes through all the lawyers at the Department of War. But it’s also – these are joint operations, so you’re operating in conjunction with another nation-state. And so when you’re conducting a joint operation in territorial waters, you have to reach an understanding as to how those operations are going to occur, and every one of these countries have their own laws, they have their own systems that they have to comply with. Some can be more aggressive than others. So I think, really, it’s a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination, but again, understand the difference between that and what you saw early last year is those were unilateral operations in international waters. These are combined operations in territorial waters, where we are working with sovereign nations in their own territorial waters. And when you do that, you have to do it based on the understandings that you have with them, and they have to comply with their own laws, their own systems, their own protocols. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Ecuador has high expectations regarding its trade relationship. We Ecuadorians have high expectations regarding what will happen with the trade relationship. We still have surcharges, and you pointed out yesterday in your column which was published in various media outlets that, as you continue to work on security issues, the scope of security measures will expand. Could we expect to have a trade agreement in the near future? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) We are working on it. And keep in mind that the tariffs aren’t specifically directed against Ecuador, they apply to all countries around the world. And the way to deal with that is through a bilateral agreement – and we’re making good progress in those negotiations. We’ve made significant progress, and I expect good news soon. That’s related, but it’s not a condition for continuing our cooperation. In terms of security – and beyond tariffs – there’s a whole range of investment opportunities. Bringing investment into this country creates jobs and at the same time, helps revive industries that were being plundered by these groups and gangs – these bandits, criminals, and terrorists who are stealing the gold, stealing the copper, stealing everything. This country’s wealth isn’t benefiting the people; it’s benefiting people who don’t even live here. And that’s also part of the economic recovery. (In English) The question was about – look, we’re engaged – it’s important to understand our tariffs on Ecuador and – it’s not on Ecuador. We have tariffs on everybody because of the 302 process. But we are engaged in talks. We’ve – they’ve progressed very well. I hope we’re going to have very good news soon. But the tariff situation is not a condition of closer economic cooperation. As an example, this is a country that has incredible critical mineral reserves. They have some of the largest copper mines in the region. They have illicit gold mining going on right now. None of this money is benefiting the people of this country. All of that is being stolen by these terrorist organizations, and the money is going into the pockets of people many of whom don’t even live in this country. They live in Spain. They’re hiding in Mexico. They don’t even live here. So part of our cooperation with them is ensuring that they can recapture and retake what belongs to the people of this country, and have professionalized operations in these mines that are environmentally sensitive, that pay the workers what they should be paid, and that the revenues from that benefit the people of this country and create jobs for the people of the country, not for a bunch of terrorists and not for a bunch of criminals who have long run roughshod – not just in Ecuador but all these other countries – oftentimes, sadly, with the cooperation of elected officials and government officials in these countries. And this administration here is putting an end to that. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, there have been three attacks on U.S. ships in – some have been very close calls, and officials — SECRETARY RUBIO: On what, naval vessels? QUESTION: On naval vessels, sorry, yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: And officials have been telling us that they’re certain that Iran is getting help. Who’s it coming from, and what is the U.S. going to do about it if they’re getting help? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know what official told you that. QUESTION: Some other official in the administration — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know. I mean, these are anonymous people. They make stuff up all the time. The truth — QUESTION: So you don’t think Iran is getting help? SECRETARY RUBIO: We don’t believe anybody is giving Iran anything that’s changing the dynamics or the parameters of what we’re seeing. At the end of the day is they continue to fire at our naval ships, and when they fire at our naval ships, they pay a price in tankers. They lose a lot of tankers. They don’t hit our ships, but they lose five tankers. They lost five more last night – four were damaged; one was sunk – so they’ll continue to pay price for that. In the meantime, we’re going to continue to strangle them economically. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, returning to the issue of boat strikes in Latin American waters, the United States has been very open about these boat strikes; it’s released videos of most of them. SECRETARY RUBIO: Mm-hmm. QUESTION: But there were three earlier this year, three boats that were blown up earlier this year, near Galapagos in Ecuadorian waters. Our reporting has found that that was a CIA covert program. Why has the United States not publicly acknowledged that, and is there any more you can say about these three (inaudible) strikes? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t – I’m not going to comment on your reporting. I don’t even know if your reporting is accurate when you say that. I can tell you that we have – we – but I’m not talking about that incident. In general, we haven’t hidden the fact that we are going to go after narco-trafficking boats. We’ve been doing it now for over a year, and now the difference is that we’re doing it in collaboration and in cooperation with – working alongside countries in the region, in their territorial waters. And in fact, some of these countries are taking the strikes themselves. So that’s what I can tell you. We’re going to continue to do it. And we’re not just going to continue to do that. These terrorist groups have to be dismantled – not just by blowing up their boats and taking their boats; they have to be dismantled financially. I don’t know if you guys fully comprehend how deeply rooted into societies these criminal bands have become. I mean, you had people in governments here that are complicit with them and what they were doing. It’s illegal mining, but it goes all the way down to the street level – murder, extortion, murder for hire, you name it. I mean, these groups became more powerful than governments in many cases. And if you don’t confront these groups, they will eat these countries alive. It’s like a cancer that continues to grow until you don’t literally have a state anymore. You become an ungovernable territory. And we don’t want to see that, they don’t want to see it, and I’m glad that we have leaders in this region that are serious about going after these groups, because if we didn’t, we would have failed country after failed country in the region. And so we’re very happy that we have partners now in this region, in Colombia, in Ecuador, in El Salvador, and in other places that are being very aggressive about taking these groups on and dismantling them before it’s too late. QUESTION: (Inaudible.) QUESTION: Did President Noboa express any concern, though, about fishermen who have been caught up in this, who have been killed or arrested? SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, I didn’t discuss it with him. I think at the end of the day these are joint operations. We’re conducting them in coordination with them. And as I said, our goal is not to go after fishermen; our goal is to go after drug traffickers. Our goal is to go after drug boats. Our goal is to go after illegal fishing and stop those from going out there. There are – there is illegal fishing. They’re raping the Galapagos. I mean, they are destroying that part of the world with illegal fishing vessels that are out there. We don’t bomb them, but we certainly want to arrest people that are involved in illegal fishing. Because again, those fisheries belong to Ecuador; they don’t belong to illegal narco-trafficking groups and these terrorist organizations. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) I don’t know if you’re concerned that, as a result of the Monroe Doctrine, there is a possibility that leftist movements might begin to emerge in Latin America. SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) The thing is that leftist movements exist in Latin America; they have existed for a long time and have ruined the countries. What have leftist movements done in this hemisphere? Nothing but misery – misery in Venezuela, misery in Cuba, misery in Nicaragua, in this country. How did all these criminal gangs get in here? In collaboration with whom? With the left, with the leftist movement. What happened with Petro in Colombia – a country that for four years was unable to fight against these criminal groups as it should have? They even have ties to those groups. So those movements already exist. What we’re not going to allow is to live in a region that eventually threatens the United States’ national security – a region with transnational groups that are more powerful than the government, armed with government weapons, drones, and a range of military technology that threatens the State and will eventually threaten the United States. (In English) The question was whether I was worried about left-wing groups or left-wing movements rising in – as a result of U.S. policy. Left-wing groups have already been here, and they’ve destroyed the hemisphere. The left wing destroyed Venezuela, the left wing destroyed Cuba, the left wing destroyed Nicaragua. The left wing has basically destroyed every country they’ve gotten a hold of in the hemisphere. Not only have they done that here in Ecuador as well, not only have they done that in Bolivia – look what Bolivia has suffered for 25 years because of left-wing governance. On – and in fact, not only did these groups destroy these countries because of bad economic policies in places like Ecuador and in Colombia over the last four years; these left-wing groups are actually in alliance with these criminal narco-trafficking organizations. They are aligned with them. They are allied with them. They permit them to conduct these activities in a nefarious alliance between them. So I’m glad that’s being confronted. And by the way, these groups are not just threats to these countries; they ultimately become threats to the United States. I work for the United States of America. And if a threat in this region is emerging to the national security and national interest of our country, we are going to address it. And what we’re very happy about is that we can now address it in partnership with other presidents and other leaders in this region that feel the same way. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — QUESTION: Secretary Rubio, if you’re talking about groups that are stronger than the state and fracturing the states, it sounds like a pretty similar situation to Mexico. What’s – what — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, Mexico’s bad. It’s a bad situation. QUESTION: So what’s the – given the fact that the Mexican Government isn’t welcoming, or draws a pretty bright line about what it will accept in terms of U.S. military involvement, how – what is the plan for that? How can you overcome that and have this kind of more tough approach that you’re describing? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s a – yeah. The case of Mexico’s a – it’s an even graver challenge because of the size of the country, because of the power of the cartels that are there. I don’t think it’s any mystery to anybody that there are territories, vast territories in Mexico that are not governed by the state; they are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations. Now, I will say this: In fairness, the Mexicans have done more than they’ve ever done before to go after these groups. But it is still not nearly enough. They know that; we’ve expressed that to them. And we hope to work cooperatively with them to do more. Because at the end, the head of the snake are these cartels in Mexico. And they are a threat to the Mexican state, and the people of Mexico will tell you that. The number one issue in Mexico, poll after poll shows, is security. Political candidates are routinely assassinated in Mexico; judges routinely assassinated; journalists who report on the cartels routinely assassinated by these groups. So these groups pose an enormous threat right on our border. They have drones now. They’re using drones to try to traffic drugs and people across the border. These groups are very dangerous, they’re very well financed, they need to be confronted. Our hope and our intent is to do it in partnership with Mexico. That’s the ideal. But eventually, that threat will have to be confronted, one way or the other. But our hope is to do it cooperatively with Mexican authorities. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Ecuador is taking action against criminal groups with support from the United States. Is there no risk of mistakes being made – for example, with the interceptions of vessels that have occurred in recent weeks in the Pacific, which have raised concerns that fishermen engaged in their work could die? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Nobody is looking to kill fishermen here. But the greatest risk is that these groups will continue to operate, because they are killing people. While some cities here are very safe, there are others with murder rates higher than any other city in the region and that poses a danger to the people. I imagine that those listening to me are familiar with some of these cities, either personally or through people they know who have been threatened, murdered, had their businesses taken away, or have suffered at the hands of these criminal gangs. We must stand up to these people; we must do something. And I’m glad there’s a President here who’s willing to take action. That is the greatest risk we face. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — SECRETARY RUBIO: All right. We got to wrap up. Quick, go. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, will you meet with Delcy Rodríguez if she comes to New York for the United Nations General Assembly? SECRETARY RUBIO: Maybe, maybe. We’ve talked quite a bit. Maybe. She’ll be there in New York. I don’t know if she’s actually going, but if she does, that probably will happen. But we haven’t scheduled anything yet. But sure, we’ve talked a bunch of times. QUESTION: Ecuador rejected foreign bases here, I think last year. Did you discuss expanding the U.S. military presence? How far would you like to – did you discuss that with Noboa today or — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we’re conducting joint operations now. We don’t necessarily need to have a base here in order to do that. They had a referendum vote last year. We didn’t discuss that today. I’m aware of the vote that they had. But the most important thing is not having a base or not having a base. We’re open to it if they change their mind. But in the interim, we’re operating – our elite forces are operating alongside one another going after these groups, and I think that’s an incredible development, and that’s an important development. That’s the only way you’re going to beat these narcotrafficking terrorists. All right. One more, and then we got to go, because — QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Ecuador has signed an agreement with the United States as a third country to receive migrants. And, as I understand it, a group from Ecuador is coming. How does that agreement work? Where will they arrive, what kind of migrants are they, and what nationalities do they have? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Well, first of all, obviously, when you make an agreement with a country, that country has the right to see a list. We send them a list of names with their backgrounds and all that information, and they decide who gets in and who doesn’t. They can veto any name. “No, I don’t accept this person.” They even control the number: 50, 20, 10. That’s up to the governments. That’s the agreement. It’s a bilateral agreement. We’re not going to send a plane full of people they don’t know and with as many people as we want. It’s a bilateral agreement. And most people who are in the United States illegally, when given the option to go to a third country or return to their own country, they return to their own country. The vast majority do so, and that is really the most important function you have in those agreements. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Where do people who are deported to a third country go? I mean, Ecuador, for example, where? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) We provide funding and assistance to help these people get settled. Eventually, I imagine these individuals will seek to return to their own countries, which, at the end of the day, is the goal. And they have the right to do so immediately. If they decide tomorrow that they’re going to return to their country, they aren’t sent to a third country; however, the countries with which we have these agreements always have the right to say, “I don’t want this person,” or “It can’t be 20, it has to be 10.” They always have that option. All right, one more and we go. (In English) All right. One more and we go. Okay, I will – all right. QUESTION: No, I have – I have one question. Yesterday, President De La Espriella was talking about his plan to expand investment and have this kind of reciprocal economic growth and investment between the United States and Colombia. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: But oftentimes, the U.S. companies haven’t invested as much as U.S. governments would have liked for – maybe because of internal regulations or for whatever reason. Do you think that the United States, the Trump Administration, can actually make the investment happen? Because I think one of the things we saw in Venezuela was that this deal that you all just finalized came after the U.S. oil majors weren’t willing to go in in the same way. What’s your thought regarding company — SECRETARY RUBIO: No. Well, first of all, that’s an inaccurate description. And these people that have reported it, they don’t know what they’re talking about. The problem is that we moved faster than the private sector on the investments in Venezuela because we had a very unique opportunity. But there are – Chevron’s already expanded their operations. There are other smaller operations that are going in. And then there are companies like Exxon that, so far, have decided not to go in because they have a long history of expropriation, and frankly, they don’t like the fields that are being offered to them, so they’d prefer not to go in. Someone else will go in. So – but the deal had nothing to do because of American companies weren’t moving fast enough. We just had a very unique opportunity to be involved in something that was beneficial to the country of the United States, who I work for, but also beneficial, in the long term especially, for the people of Venezuela. In the case of Colombia, look, attracting investment there – obviously, there’s always going to be security concerns. If you don’t have security, no one’s going to invest in the country – security meaning physical security, but also legal security. Is the government stable? Are the laws going to be applied? That’s always important. And I think with a new president and a new administration a lot of that is going to be solved. And then there’s just the mechanisms – identifying investment opportunities and pairing the investment opportunity with the American company. I think in the case of Colombia it’s going to be less problematic, because there has been a long history of American investment in Colombia already. And I think the only thing we’re working through is there are some programs – whether it’s Millennium Challenge, whether it’s some of our investment funds – that can serve as a catalyst for some of that investment to happen. So we’re trying to identify whether some of these programs can be used to serve as a catalyst to speed up that investment and that economic recuperation, especially in areas that involve critical minerals and energy. Okay? QUESTION: Thanks. SECRETARY RUBIO: Natural gas – natural gas is important. Okay, guys. Thank you. QUESTION: Thank you. title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with José Manuel Acevedo of RCN
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio with José Manuel Acevedo of RCN Interview Marco Rubio, Secretary of State September 8, 2026 Via Teleconference September 9, 2026 (Via translation.) QUESTION: Well, it is a tremendous honor to have with us here at RCN and NTN24 the United States Secretary of State, Marco Rubio. Secretary, thank you for being here with us. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, thanks. It’s a great honor to be with you as well. QUESTION: They are also watching us in Miami and throughout Latin America thanks to NTN24. As you know, we are networks that have followed your work closely since you were a senator and now as Secretary of State. And now you come to a country like Colombia, one that is not unfamiliar to you, because it must be said that you have defended democracy in our country, Colombia. Additionally, if you’ll allow me a personal question, your wife also has very deep roots in this country. What is your personal connection to Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, my wife—her mother was born in [inaudible], stayed in [inaudible], and then moved to Bogotá. She still has relatives here. And I live in Miami, and I don’t know if you know this, but there are a lot of Colombians in Miami. QUESTION: Lots of them. SECRETARY RUBIO: And that’s why I wanted to mention it. And in Broward as well. But I have always followed Colombia very closely for two reasons. The personal connection is always important, and we follow everything that happens in the country very closely because of that relationship, but also because of the relationship between our two countries. You have to understand that for more than 20 years, throughout my entire time in the Senate, for example, the most important partner we had in South America was Colombia, the most consistent one. There were changes of government in different places, but when it came to economic and security matters, the most important partner the United States had was Colombia. That was broken over the last four years. Unfortunately, although many relationships still existed at the military and security levels and so forth, we went through a period that, I would say, was not natural in our relationship. It was somewhat damaged, unfortunately. But now we are entering a new stage, and I believe we are quickly going to recover what we had—and not simply recover what we had. We are going to be able to expand it even further, because you have a president here who has tremendous enthusiasm, a lot of energy, a lot of vision, and who is willing to take risks, but who is also responsible and knows the American system well. He understands well how our system works. That is also going to help him greatly in building that connection. QUESTION: In fact, I remember you saying, “The best days are yet to come for Colombia,” after your meeting with Abelardo de la Espriella, and I imagine you still feel the same way. But for that to happen, we need cooperation, especially on an issue that I know has long been a concern for both you and the President: security. How do you view the security situation in Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: I have said it, and I will continue to say it. The most important responsibility of any government, at any level—municipal, departmental, state, as we say in the United States, or at the federal or national level—is security. It is the most important thing the government does: security. The security of a country, the security of a community, the security, the security of its people, and that is the most important thing. And to a certain extent, I think that was somewhat neglected in the thinking of the previous government over the last three or four years. You have a president who was very clearly elected, who made it very clear during his campaign and has made it clear now as president that his number one priority is to restore stability and security for the Colombian people, and we are going to help in every way possible. On top of that foundation of security comes prosperity. Prosperity is impossible without security. It is impossible to invest in a country that is unsafe. It is impossible to invest in a country that is dominated by cartels or criminal gangs. In many cases, these are not just Colombian criminal gangs; they are transnational, operating in Ecuador, Mexico, and other countries in the region. So, for us, security is fundamental. It is the most fundamental thing a government does, and these threats affect us as well, so we are going to help in every way possible. But it is not just about security; it is about security and prosperity. The two go together. QUESTION: Look, Secretary, we are being attacked with drones by illegal armed groups, and in that regard, support with technology and upgrading equipment that is already obsolete in Colombia is very important. But there is another issue that is also of great concern, and that is the attacks coming from the other side of the border. You know that Venezuela has granted impunity to many of those criminals. What can the United States do on both fronts? Technological and Venezuela. And the criminals? SECRETARY RUBIO: Let’s talk first about the situation in Venezuela. We have the ELN and the president of the FARC operating openly and with impunity from Venezuelan territory. This has been going on for more than 10, 15 years. That has to be resolved. We have made that clear to the interim authorities in Venezuela, and I think that is going to be key to improving relations between the two countries. It is impossible for relations to truly improve while that issue remains as it is. No country can allow criminal gangs and terrorists to operate with impunity on the other side of its border, attack within its national territory, and then return under the protection of another country’s borders. That cannot be allowed, and we are going to help with that. And we have already spoken with the Venezuelan authorities, including on the issue of drones. The technology is a global threat. This is a global threat because there is a lot of military equipment that requires a government with millions of dollars in order to acquire it. But in the case of these drones, that really is not necessary. Even criminal gangs can possess them and use them to attack and threaten a state. So, one of the things that is needed worldwide, not just in Colombia, is to establish new, modern defenses against this new threat, specifically drones that use fiber optics, which pose an enormous danger because at this time there is no conventional defense against them. So we have already had discussions about that. QUESTION: And is the United States willing to help Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes, but we are not only willing to help Colombia; we also need it for our own resources. So, both countries have an interest in developing the new technology necessary to prevent this type of attack and defend against it. QUESTION: Secretary, during the previous administration of President Gustavo Petro, the United States decertified us in the fight against drugs. How close are we to, or how far are we from, being certified again? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, remember that the certification announced this year has to do with the actions that took place last year. We have a completely different view when it comes to the new president and the new administration, this team. So I expect that if they continue to follow through and continue doing what they say they are going to do and what they have already done—I mean, in the last month we have seen more concrete action against these criminal groups than we possibly saw in four years. So I think that if they continue on that path, there is no doubt that the certification will change, as it has in the past. QUESTION: How soon or how far away is that? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s done on an annual basis. It’s possible that it can be done earlier because there’s a waiver process to be able to do it sooner. QUESTION: Are you going to help us in that, I imagine? SECRETARY RUBIO: I, I, what I—I’m going to do everything possible to help Colombia. And obviously, if the new government continues as it already is, it’s not that they’re making promises; they’re already doing it, and they have begun acting against that. I expect that to change. QUESTION: Secretary, there is another issue that is also of great concern to small, large, and medium-sized businesses, and I’m sure it has come up in the conversations you have had over the past month and in the one you had today in Barranquilla. The issue of tariffs on certain products is affecting us. Uh, they are asking for a temporary suspension of some of those tariffs. Are you leaving us with that good news, or are we not there yet? SECRETARY RUBIO: The tariffs, first of all, apply to everyone. They are not specifically directed at Colombia. This is worldwide. The Supreme Court and its ruling against the President’s policy required a change in strategy and the use of a new process, Section 302, which is a U.S. domestic process that is very legal, very, very technical. But the President wants to change that. The way this issue can be resolved is through a bilateral agreement between the two countries, and negotiations on that are underway. I believe there have been two rounds of negotiations, they have progressed very well, and I hope that very soon the issue can be resolved through that agreement between the two countries. And for President Trump, it is a priority. He has said so. He wants to follow through and bring this to a conclusion. He wants to reach a bilateral agreement that eliminates the problem we currently have with the tariffs. QUESTION: Well, that’s good. Hopefully that will be the case. Secretary, I know you are very diplomatic, and you are going to tell me that you cannot say much about the OFAC list and former officials such as President Petro, Armando Benedetti, and others. But tell me, are there any ongoing investigations by the United States into that? SECRETARY RUBIO: It’s not that I’m being diplomatic; I cannot offer opinions or comment on investigations, whether active or not. I cannot comment on that. What I can tell you is that with all these sanctions, in our system there is no sanction that is imposed without evidence, and the evidence is not going to be ignored. If there is evidence that someone has committed a crime, is committing a crime, or has caused harm, that will be pursued. That is not up to me. QUESTION: Are there any active investigations underway? SECRETARY RUBIO: I can’t comment on that because investigations are not under my purview. They are handled by the Department of Justice. So, I cannot comment on whether there are or are not. What I can tell you is that no one ends up on the, on the OFAC list because someone made something up. To be placed on the OFAC list, there have to be facts, there has to be evidence, there have to be concrete things that justify that decision. QUESTION: In the case of these officials. SECRETARY RUBIO: And there may possibly be others who are placed on that list at some point, if there is evidence against them as well. QUESTION: Look, on that note, Gustavo Petro used to say that you had misinformed President Donald Trump. Gustavo Petro is no longer in Colombia; he is no longer the president of Colombia. What does Marco Rubio think of Gustavo Petro? SECRETARY RUBIO: I think he is no longer president, and we are going to deal with the president you have. He is someone I have known for several years, since before he entered politics. I joked earlier that he went crazy and got into politics. But he is someone who was elected by the people of this country and someone we are going to work with. QUESTION: Just so you know, President Abelardo responded, “And you’re next.” SECRETARY RUBIO: Something like that, I think. I didn’t quite understand it; I didn’t see it very clearly, but he—but I had already been in politics for many years. He wasn’t a politician; he had never been a politician. He was interested in politics, but he wasn’t a politician. I knew him as a local businessman in Miami, and then he wanted to contribute to his country, he wanted to help his country. He ran for president when no one thought he was going to win, and he won. And now he is president, and he is the one we are going to deal with. I’m not going to dwell on the past. QUESTION: Look, I know time is short. We’re wrapping up now, Secretary, I promise. But let me ask you about a country that is, close to you, which is Cuba, and also about Nicaragua. What can the United States, and the world, do to finally bring those dictatorships to an end? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, as in every country, first, the primary responsibility for changing a system lies with the people of those countries. That is always the case. Obviously, we do not support what is happening, or what they are doing, in Nicaragua, and we have imposed sanctions against individuals, people who are contributing to the situation that currently exists in Nicaragua. When it comes to Cuba, what we are not going to continue allowing is for a military company called GAESA to keep stealing Cuba’s money, and that is why we have imposed the strongest sanctions in the history of our relationship with Cuba. Tragically, the Cuban people are suffering, but they are not suffering because of us. They are suffering for two reasons. First, because the individuals in charge of that regime are following an economic model that does not work and has never worked. But now it does not work because they have become accustomed, for more than 60 years, to living off assistance from abroad. First, it was the Soviet Union, then it was Hugo Chávez, and when the free oil they were stealing from Venezuela ran out, they were left without oil. That is not our fault. That is their fault for not having a functioning market. And second, because some—many of the leaders in Cuba who are currently part of that regime are incompetent. They do not know how to manage the economy, and they are the ones who have directly contributed to the suffering of the Cuban people. But what we are not going to allow is for them to continue evading sanctions in order to benefit themselves at the expense of the Cuban people. QUESTION: And what do you mean by not allowing it? Carrying out an operation like the one in Venezuela? SECRETARY RUBIO: Not allowing it—well, for example, we are already doing that. We have shut down bank accounts. Many, many foreign companies have left Cuba because of these sanctions, and they have left because those companies were partners, they had entered into business dealings with these elements of the regime, and they were enriching themselves. QUESTION: But could tougher measures be coming, Secretary? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m not going to speculate about what those measures might be, but we always have the right to operate and take action to protect the national security of the United States. I’m not going to comment specifically on exactly what can be done, but we have an obligation to protect the national security of the United States if a threat arises in Cuba, Venezuela, or anywhere else in the world. QUESTION: Look, one thing: the possibility of having U.S. military bases in Colombia, yes or no? SECRETARY RUBIO: Anything is possible. Obviously, this has to come through—first, we have to be invited, because this is a sovereign country, and the decision has to be made by the Venezuelan people through—sorry, by the Colombian people, through their elected officials. If they officially make that request to us, then it will be considered to see what is possible. At the end of the day, that decision is up to the President, through the U.S. Department of Defense, the Department of War. But what I can tell you, without a doubt, is that the security relationship between the United States and Colombia is not going to be the same as before; it is going to be better. QUESTION: Look, I’ll wrap up, but as we say here in Colombia, President Abelardo de la Espriella gave me the task to ask you about your political future. The 2028 elections. Am I interviewing one of the strongest candidates for 2028? SECRETARY RUBIO: But I’m not a candidate for anything right now, and I’m 100% focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs. I have my job as Secretary of State, and I also work as the President’s National Security Advisor, so I have plenty of work right now. QUESTION: But is the dream of becoming President of the United States there? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time. I’m 100% focused on my jobs. QUESTION: Secretary, and speaking of that job, we want to thank you, on behalf of all Colombians, for what you have done for this country and for its democracy. And please, continue to keep in mind cooperation based on equality, trust, and respect between the United States and Colombia. Thank you, Marco Rubio. SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you very much.
